The greatest possible value of \(\gcd(n+7, 2n+1)\) is found using the Euclidean algorithm:

\[
\gcd(n+7, 2n+1) = \gcd(n+7, 2n+1 - 2(n+7)) = \gcd(n+7, -13) = \gcd(n+7, 13).
\]

Since 13 is prime, the gcd can only be 1 or 13. It equals 13 whenever \(n+7\) is a multiple of 13, i.e., \(n \equiv 6 \pmod{13}\). For example, \(n = 6\) gives \(n+7 = 13\) and \(2n+1 = 13\), so \(\gcd(13, 13) = 13\). Thus the maximum is 13.

Answer: 13
